sentences: For most of history, reading was something people did out loud.
Silent reading was rare enough that writers sometimes remarked on it when they saw it.
Monks in the early libraries murmured as they copied, and a room full of readers sounded like a room full of bees.
Part of the reason was practical.
Old manuscripts often ran words together with no spaces, and sounding a line out was the easiest way to find where one word ended and the next began.
Part of it was social.
Books were expensive, so one person read while a household or a workshop listened.
In cigar factories in the Caribbean and later in Florida, workers paid a reader out of their own wages to read newspapers and novels during long shifts.
The readers sat on raised platforms and performed every voice in the story.
Some factory owners tried to ban them, and the workers went on strike to keep them.
Printing changed the economics, and cheap books moved reading into private rooms.
Spaces between words, punctuation, and paragraphs made silent reading easier, and over a few centuries the quiet reader became the normal reader.
Reading aloud never disappeared, though.
Parents still read to children at bedtime, and teachers still read to classrooms.
Radio brought serialized stories into kitchens, and audiobooks later turned long commutes into time for novels.
Machines began reading aloud much later, and for a long time they sounded like machines.
Early synthetic voices were built from rules, and every sentence came out with the same flat rhythm.
They were good enough to be useful and tiring enough that few people listened for long.
That gap matters most to the people who depend on these voices every day.
A blind student reading a textbook, or someone with dyslexia working through a contract, does not get to choose a different format.
For them, a better voice is not a novelty.
It is the difference between an hour of work and an afternoon of fatigue.
Modern voices are learned from recordings rather than written as rules, and the best of them pause, lift, and land the way a careful reader would.
What used to need a data center can now run on a laptop, and soon on a phone in a pocket.
If that holds, the oldest way of reading could become available to anyone with a screen.
